title.narrative: RS! Sierra Leone Cocoa

description.narrative: To contribute to a sustainable and inclusive cocoa value chain, in which producers receive a fair value, and work in safe conditions, without the use child labour and land rights and forest are protected in Sierra Leone.The main objectives of the project are The target groups are producers organisations, women in cocoa, agriculture workers unionObjectives 1. To create, strengthen and/or join in dialogue to enhance access to knowledge, information and credible evidence, where vulnerable groups are included and policy makers can make informed decisions. 2. To strengthen the ability of civil society to claim and defend their rights and influence decision making 3. To mobilise activate and engage citizens and CSOs to change norms and influence the policy agenda for the range of issues highlighted in the problem analysis

comment.narrative: Now more women and men are claiming and defending their land rights in the law courts. One woman farmer specifically cited and linked her understanding and confidence of the Lands Act to our awareness campaign. This was confirmed by our partner � Women in Media � who was in court with the woman. The Minister of Lands has confirmed that the Lands Act is being implemented better. He said currently, they're using GPS to digitise all lands into a database to resolve land disputes. He also announced the establishment of a dedicated regional police desk, the 'Anti-Lands Office,' to specifically address land-related issues. He said listening to lands awareness campaigns on the radio together with their internal information help them c better understand land matters and act in addressing the issues

# and qualitative description of new or improved governmental policies implemented for sustainable production, trade and/or consumption

comment.narrative: The Customary Land, National Land Commission Act, and Rights Act and the GEWE Act are being implemented better particularly for women. Community chiefs have allocated over 90 hectares of land with full ownership rights to women’s groups in Peama Town, Looma, Gandom, and Muloma, marking a major milestone in gender-responsive land governance. Individual women farmers such as Sir Lasana, Bobo Fatoma, Mami Lansana, and Madi Jah have acquired and are cultivating land for cocoa and oil palm, demonstrating increased agency in agricultural production
